key_sub: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
body_html:
How to think about it

A scalar has only size (distance, speed, time); a vector has size and direction (displacement, velocity, acceleration). Displacement is the change in position; velocity = displacement/time; acceleration a = Δv/Δt.

On a position–time graph the gradient is the velocity; on a velocity–time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area under the graph is the displacement. For constant acceleration: v = u + aΔt, Δx = uΔt + ½aΔt² and v² = u² + 2aΔx.

Example

A car goes from 0 to 20 m·s⁻¹ in 5 s. Acceleration?

a = Δv/Δt

Answer: 4 m·s⁻²

Example

You walk 3 m east and 3 m west. Displacement?

Directions cancel.

Answer: 0 m

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up distance and displacement.
  • Thinking a negative acceleration always means slowing down.
  • Reading the gradient of a position–time graph as acceleration.
